newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling hits record low ahead of strike.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling hits record low ahead of strike.

text.p: Kenya's shilling sank to a record official low against the dollar on Thursday, as the government branded as illegal a national strike called for Friday, raising fears of clashes between police and supporters of reform.
On the industrial front, a go-slow by Kenyan air traffic controllers ended with agreement with the government and flights returned to normal after five days of cancellations and delays.

The shilling, extending the slide that began when the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a key aid package last week citing corruption, fell 4.08 percent on Thursday to close at a commercial average of 70.26 to the dollar.

Dealers said the central bank sold dollars above 71 to slow the fall. The shilling has lost 18.08 percent since the IMF halted a key aid package a week ago, citing the government's failure to crack down on corruption.
Its last official low against the dollar was 69.22 in 1993.

Commercial dealers said investors were alarmed by President Daniel arap Moi's reaction to the IMF decision. On Tuesday he played down the impact of the IMF ruling, urging Kenyans to become self-reliant and saying the lost IMF loans were insignificant in relation to Kenya's overall economy.
Moi, 73, and in power for 19 years, has yet to name a date for a general election which must be held this year.

Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's statement that the government was considering talks with the IMF on securing a second year of the three-year loan package did not prevent the shilling's slide.The overall IMF package was worth $205 million.
Worries in the foreign exchange market were compounded by a call for a nationwide general strike on Friday by an opposition-backed alliance of groups demanding constitutional reforms.

Organisers urged supporters to rally in a park in the heart of Nairobi and in 11 other towns on Friday. Labour Minister Philip Masinde declared the strike illegal and urged police to ensure Friday was a normal day.
"The strike is going to be unlawful and it is an offence to participate in such activities, just as it is unlawful for anyone to incite workers to go out on strike," he said.
"I would like to advise as well as appeal to the workers all over the country not to take the law into their own hands, to ignore the strike call and continue to do their work," he said.
Masinde's statement appeared to set the stage for clashes between supporters of reform and riot police, as the strike organisers have called for marches in support of the stoppage.
The United Nations said its offices in central Nairobi would be closed on Friday and buses that usually take most of its employees to offices outside the city centre would not run.

Embassies said they would not take action against employees who joined the strike and many shops in the city were expected to close. One Nairobi law firm told employees they could take the day off, but only as leave either to strike or stay at home.

At least nine people were killed on July 7 in clashes between police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and other centres. The clashes, the worst political violence in seven years, rattled investors and tourists.
Moi's government has offered a set of minimal changes before the elections and a constitutional review after the elections and has managed to dent opposition support for the strike.
Masinde said the government could not discount violence on Friday as a few people appeared bent on breaking the law.
At the same news conference, Masinde announced the go-slow by Kenyan air traffic controllers since Saturday had ended.
"The situation is back to normal. We have explained what the government is trying to do and they (controllers) have understood and cooperated," he said but did not give details.
Air controllers said they returned to normal work after being assured a report Moi received on Wednesday on conditions of service for government workers would meet their concerns.

They said the head of the civil service had assured them on Thursday that details of the report would be released in two weeks. They said if the promises fell short of their demands they would either resume the go-slow or start another action.
The air traffic controllers had demanded a 50-fold increase in what they say is pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
